newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan, Israel, revive Aqaba "peace airport" plans.
newsitem.headline: Jordan, Israel, revive Aqaba "peace airport" plans.

text.p: Jordan and Israel are working on a $30 million expansion plan to turn Jordan's southern Aqaba airport into a Red Sea "peace airport", run jointly by both countries, a senior Jordanian aviation official said on Monday.

Captain Jasser al-Zayad, head of Jordan's Civil Aviation Authority, said the two countries planned to start diverting international flights to Aqaba from the nearby Israeli beach resort of Eilat by the end of August.
"In principle, we are moving towards experimental operation within three months of the joint Jordanian-Israeli peace airport," Zayad told Reuters.

The project, announced in the wake of the 1994 Jordan-Israel peace treaty, has been stalled for months but received fresh impetus from a secret summit last week between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Jordan's King Hussein.
It calls for expanding Aqaba airport's facilities to eventually divert all Eilat's international flights, about 150 a month, leaving the congested airport to domestic Israeli traffic, Zayad said.
Jordanian-Israeli officials are scheduled to meet in Aqaba on May 27 and 28 to review progress and discuss setting up a joint Israeli-Jordanian management firm, Zayad said.

"We are discussing setting up a joint holding company to manage and operate the airport on a commercial basis which could be a semi-government owned or private sector. All the options are open," Zayad said.

Interest in the project, a brainchild of Crown Prince Hassan and former Israeli Prime Minster Shimon Peres appeared to have receded after Netanyahu's government expressed security concerns and fears the project was an expensive political gesture.
The project to transfer flights from Eilat to Aqaba, just nine km (six miles) away, was the first major joint Israeli-Jordanian venture announced after the 1994 treaty.
It would allow Aqaba airport to handle nearly 300,000 international passengers annually, or nearly 20 times the current levels.

Aqaba airport handled last year a total of 72,634 passengers of whom 57,192 were carried on the domestic Aqaba-Amman route and just 15,442 were foreign visitors. The airport handled a total of 2,925 flights in 1996, only 365 flights which were international.

But Aqaba will initially only be able to receive around two to three extra daily flights -- less than half of Eilat's international traffic -- until expansion of the terminal, fuel tanks and infrastructure are completed.

Zayad said the project was economically beneficial to Jordan, bringing more passenger traffic, employing additional labour, and putting Aqaba on the international tourist map -- even if most tourists were heading straight across to Israel.

He said the two sides will examine various financing options for a $30 million expansion cost, scaled down from an original $116 million estimated by U.S. consultants Lockheed Martin Corp, which was rejected as too high by the two sides.
The firm was given a grant in 1995 by the U.S. government to undertake the feasibility study for the project.
